## Names
The spelling _Babylon_ is the Latin representation of [Koine Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koine_Greek "Koine Greek")_Babylṓn_ ([Βαβυλών](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%CE%92%CE%B1%CE%B2%CF%85%CE%BB%CF%8E%CE%BD "wikt:Βαβυλών")), derived from the native [Akkadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akkadian_language "Akkadian language"): 𒆍𒀭𒊏𒆠, romanized:_Bābilim_, [lit.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation")'gate of the [god(s)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_(deity) "El (deity)")'.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylon#cite_note-Lambert2011-15) The [cuneiform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuneiform "Cuneiform") spelling is _KÁ.DIG̃IR.RA KI_, corresponding to the Sumerian phrase _Kan dig̃irak_.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylon#cite_note-16) The sign 𒆍 (_KÁ_) is the logogram for "gate", 𒀭 (_[DIG̃IR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dingir "Dingir")_) means "god", and 𒊏 (_RA_) represents the [coda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syllabic_coda "Syllabic coda") of the word _dig̃ir_ (-r) followed by the genitive suffix _-ak_. The final 𒆠 ([KI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ki_(cuneiform) "Ki (cuneiform)")) is a determinative indicating that the previous signs are to be understood as a place name.

**Raja Ravi Varma** (Malayalam:[[ɾaːd͡ʒaː ɾɐʋi ʋɐrmːɐ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Malayalam "Help:IPA/Malayalam")) (29 April 1848 – 2 October 1906[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-4)) was an Indian painter. His works are one of the best examples of the fusion of European [academic art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_art "Academic art") with a purely Indian sensibility and iconography. He greatly enhanced his reach and influence as a painter and public figure by making affordable [lithographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithography "Lithography") of his paintings available to the public. His lithographs increased the involvement of common people with fine arts and defined artistic tastes. His religious depictions of Hindu deities and works from [Indian epic poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_epic_poetry "Indian epic poetry") and [Puranas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puranas "Puranas") have received critical acclaim. He was part of the royal family of [Parappanad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parappanad "Parappanad"), [Malappuram district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malappuram_district "Malappuram district").
Raja Ravi Varma was closely related to the royal family of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") of present-day [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala") state in India. Later in his life, two of his granddaughters were adopted into the royal family.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-5)

Varma was born on 29 April 1848, as [M. R. Ry.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maha_Raja_Rajya_Shri "Maha Raja Rajya Shri") Ravi Varma ([Malayalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayalam_language "Malayalam language"): രവി വർമ്മ), [Koil Thampuran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koyi_Thampuran "Koyi Thampuran") of Kilimanoor at [Kilimanoor palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_palace "Kilimanoor palace") in the erstwhile [princely state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princely_state "Princely state") of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") (present-day [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala"))[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-pal-6) into an aristocratic family that for over 200 years produced consorts for the princesses of the matrilineal Travancore royal family. The title [Raja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja "Raja") was conferred as a personal title by the Viceroy and Governor-General of India [Lord Curzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Curzon "Lord Curzon").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-pal-6)

Varma's sister-in-law, [Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharani_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi "Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi"), Senior Rani of [Attingal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal "Attingal") (or [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Travancore "Kingdom of Travancore")), who adopted Varma's granddaughters in 1900

Ravi Varma was the son of Ezhumavil Neelakanthan Bhattatiripad and Uma Ambabayi Thampurratti. His mother Uma Ambabayi Thampuratty belonged to the baronial family which ruled the Kilimanoor [feudal estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") within the kingdom of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore"). She was a poet and writer, and her work _Parvati Swayamvaram_ was published by Varma after her death. Ravi Varma's father was a scholar of [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit") and [Ayurveda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayurveda "Ayurveda") and hailed from the [Ernakulam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernakulam "Ernakulam") district in Kerala. Ravi Varma had two siblings, a sister named [Mangala Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangala_Bayi "Mangala Bayi") and a brother named [Raja Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Raja_Raja_Varma "C. Raja Raja Varma") (born 1860). The last-named was also a painter and worked closely with Ravi Varma all his life.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1866, at age 18, Varma was married to 12-year-old Bhageerthi Bayi (known formally as Pooruruttati Nal Bhageerathi Bayi Thampuratty) of the royal house of [Mavelikkara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mavelikkara "Mavelikkara"), another major [fief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") of Travancore kingdom. Notably, the house of Mavellikara was a branch of the Royal House of Travancore. Bhageerthi was the youngest of three sisters; her two elder siblings were adopted into the royal family of Travancore in 1857 to perpetuate the lineage. Designated the Senior and Junior Rani of Attingal, their descendants were vested with the succession to the throne of Travancore. Therefore, Ravi Varma's connection to the royal family became very close due to his marriage with Bhageerthi. His children would be royal by birth, since they belonged to their mother's family. The marriage, which was arranged by the parents in the proper Indian manner, was considered successful. The couple had five children, two sons, and three daughters. Their elder son, Kerala Varma (b.1876) was of an excessively spiritual temperament. He never married and eventually renounced the world, leaving home for good in 1912. The younger son, Rama Varma (born 1879), inherited his father's artistic talent and studied at the [JJ School of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JJ_School_of_Arts "JJ School of Arts"), [Mumbai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumbai "Mumbai"). He was married to Gowri Kunjamma, sister of [Dewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewan "Dewan")[PGN Unnithan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGN_Unnithan "PGN Unnithan"), and became the father of seven children.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The three daughters of Ravi Varma and Bhageerthi Bayi were Mahaprabha Amma (who features in two of Varma's most famous paintings), Uma Amma (named after Varma's mother) and Cheria Kochamma. In 1900 CE, the Royal House of Travancore once again faced a succession crisis. Bhageerthi's two elder sisters, who had been adopted in order to carry forward the lineage, had failed to produce the desired heirs. They had six children between them, but only two of those survived, and both were boys (who also, incidentally, later died childless). According to the [matrilineal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrilineal "Matrilineal") Marumakkathayam system, the succession to the throne could only progress through females, and therefore it was necessary to make an adoption. Tradition dictated that two girls belonging to branches of the Royal Family be adopted together. They would be designated the Senior and Junior Rani of Attingal, and the succession to the throne of Travancore would be vested in their progeny, in accordance with the unusual and unique [Marumakkathayam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marumakkathayam "Marumakkathayam") system of succession.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Two of Varma's granddaughters were marked by destiny to receive this honour, the main reason being that they were the nearest matrilineal ([cognatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognatic "Cognatic")) kin to the incumbent Rani of Attingal. In August 1900, Mahaprabha's eldest daughter Lakshmi Bayi (aged 5 years) and Uma's eldest daughter Parvati Bayi (aged 4 years) were adopted into the Royal family of Travancore. It was [Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharani_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi "Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi"), their surviving grand-aunt, who formally adopted them. She died within one year of doing this, and the two girls were then installed as the Senior and Junior Ranis of [Attingal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal "Attingal") respectively. They were married while yet in their early teens to two gentlemen from suitable aristocratic families. It was the Junior Rani, [Sethu Parvathi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sethu_Parvathi_Bayi "Sethu Parvathi Bayi"), who gave birth to the much-awaited heir in 1912, exactly a day after her sixteenth birthday. Incidentally, her husband was a grand-nephew of Raja Ravi Varma and belonged to [Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_Palace "Kilimanoor Palace"). The newborn child was the future Maharaja [Chithira Thirunal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chithira_Thirunal_Balarama_Varma "Chithira Thirunal Balarama Varma"), the last ruling [Maharaja of Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharaja_of_Travancore "Maharaja of Travancore").

He was followed by a brother (the future Maharaja [Marthanda Varma III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uthradom_Thirunal_Marthanda_Varma "Uthradom Thirunal Marthanda Varma")) and a sister [Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karthika_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi "Karthika Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi"), the mother of Maharaja [Rama Varma VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moolam_Thirunal_Rama_Varma "Moolam Thirunal Rama Varma") who is presently on the throne (since 2013). Meanwhile, the Senior Rani ([Sethu Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sethu_Lakshmi_Bayi "Sethu Lakshmi Bayi"), daughter of Mahaprabha Amma, and Regent from 1924 to 1931) also gave birth to two daughters later in life (in 1923 and 1926).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
In this way, the entire present (existing) royal family of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") is descended from Raja Ravi Varma. Well known among his royal descendants are the writers [Aswathi Thirunal Gowri Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswathi_Thirunal_Gowri_Lakshmi_Bayi "Aswathi Thirunal Gowri Lakshmi Bayi") and [Shreekumar Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shreekumar_Varma "Shreekumar Varma"), the artist [Rukmini Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rukmini_Varma "Rukmini Varma") and the classical musician [Aswathi Thirunal Rama Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswathi_Thirunal_Rama_Varma "Aswathi Thirunal Rama Varma").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Around Ravi Varma's 57th birthday he announced his decision to accept [Sanyasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanyasa "Sanyasa"), and retire from all worldly life when he turned 60. In his final years he suffered from grief for the death of Raja Raja Varma, and also from diabetes, which contributed to his death on 2 October 1906.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
Varma was patronised by [Ayilyam Thirunal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayilyam_Thirunal "Ayilyam Thirunal"), the next [Maharaja of Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharaja_of_Travancore "Maharaja of Travancore") and began formal training thereafter.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-The_Diary_of_C._Rajaraja_Varma-7) He learned the basics of painting in [Madurai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madurai "Madurai"). Later, he was trained in water painting by Rama Swami Naidu and rather reluctantly in [oil painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_painting "Oil painting") by British portraitist Theodore Jenson.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-8)
[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Raja_Ravi_Verma_Studio_Vadodara.jpg/250px-Raja_Ravi_Verma_Studio_Vadodara.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raja_Ravi_Verma_Studio_Vadodara.jpg)
The studio used by Varma during his stay at the [Laxmi Vilas Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laxmi_Vilas_Palace "Laxmi Vilas Palace")

The British administrator, [Edgar Thurston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Thurston "Edgar Thurston") was significant in promoting the careers of Varma and his brother.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-9) Varma received widespread acclaim after he won an award for an exhibition of his paintings at Vienna in 1873. Varma's paintings were also sent to the [World's Columbian Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition") held in Chicago in 1893 and he was awarded three gold medals.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-10) He travelled throughout India in search of subjects. He often modelled Hindu [Goddesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goddess "Goddess") on [Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_India "South India") women, whom he considered beautiful. Ravi Varma is particularly noted for his paintings depicting episodes from the story of [Dushyanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dushyanta "Dushyanta") and [Shakuntala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakuntala "Shakuntala"), and [Nala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nala "Nala") and [Damayanti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damayanti "Damayanti"), from the [Mahabharata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabharata "Mahabharata"). Ravi Varma's representation of [Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu "Hindu") characters has become a part of the Indian imagination of the epics. He is often criticized for being too showy and sentimental in his style but his work remains very popular in India. Many of his fabulous paintings are housed at [Laxmi Vilas Palace, Vadodara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laxmi_Vilas_Palace,_Vadodara "Laxmi Vilas Palace, Vadodara").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-11)

**Raja Ravi Varma** (Malayalam:[[ɾaːd͡ʒaː ɾɐʋi ʋɐrmːɐ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Malayalam "Help:IPA/Malayalam")) (29 April 1848 – 2 October 1906[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-4)) was an Indian painter. His works are one of the best examples of the fusion of European [academic art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_art "Academic art") with a purely Indian sensibility and iconography. He greatly enhanced his reach and influence as a painter and public figure by making affordable [lithographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithography "Lithography") of his paintings available to the public. His lithographs increased the involvement of common people with fine arts and defined artistic tastes. His religious depictions of Hindu deities and works from [Indian epic poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_epic_poetry "Indian epic poetry") and [Puranas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puranas "Puranas") have received critical acclaim. He was part of the royal family of [Parappanad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parappanad "Parappanad"), [Malappuram district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malappuram_district "Malappuram district").
Raja Ravi Varma was closely related to the royal family of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") of present-day [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala") state in India. Later in his life, two of his granddaughters were adopted into the royal family.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-5)

He was followed by a brother (the future Maharaja [Marthanda Varma III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uthradom_Thirunal_Marthanda_Varma "Uthradom Thirunal Marthanda Varma")) and a sister [Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karthika_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi "Karthika Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi"), the mother of Maharaja [Rama Varma VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moolam_Thirunal_Rama_Varma "Moolam Thirunal Rama Varma") who is presently on the throne (since 2013). Meanwhile, the Senior Rani ([Sethu Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sethu_Lakshmi_Bayi "Sethu Lakshmi Bayi"), daughter of Mahaprabha Amma, and Regent from 1924 to 1931) also gave birth to two daughters later in life (in 1923 and 1926).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
In this way, the entire present (existing) royal family of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") is descended from Raja Ravi Varma. Well known among his royal descendants are the writers [Aswathi Thirunal Gowri Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswathi_Thirunal_Gowri_Lakshmi_Bayi "Aswathi Thirunal Gowri Lakshmi Bayi") and [Shreekumar Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shreekumar_Varma "Shreekumar Varma"), the artist [Rukmini Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rukmini_Varma "Rukmini Varma") and the classical musician [Aswathi Thirunal Rama Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswathi_Thirunal_Rama_Varma "Aswathi Thirunal Rama Varma").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Around Ravi Varma's 57th birthday he announced his decision to accept [Sanyasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanyasa "Sanyasa"), and retire from all worldly life when he turned 60. In his final years he suffered from grief for the death of Raja Raja Varma, and also from diabetes, which contributed to his death on 2 October 1906.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
Varma was patronised by [Ayilyam Thirunal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayilyam_Thirunal "Ayilyam Thirunal"), the next [Maharaja of Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharaja_of_Travancore "Maharaja of Travancore") and began formal training thereafter.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-The_Diary_of_C._Rajaraja_Varma-7) He learned the basics of painting in [Madurai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madurai "Madurai"). Later, he was trained in water painting by Rama Swami Naidu and rather reluctantly in [oil painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_painting "Oil painting") by British portraitist Theodore Jenson.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-8)

Varma's paintings were also sent to the [World's Columbian Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition") held in Chicago in 1893 and he was awarded three gold medals.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-10) He travelled throughout India in search of subjects. He often modelled Hindu [Goddesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goddess "Goddess") on [Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_India "South India") women, whom he considered beautiful. Ravi Varma is particularly noted for his paintings depicting episodes from the story of [Dushyanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dushyanta "Dushyanta") and [Shakuntala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakuntala "Shakuntala"), and [Nala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nala "Nala") and [Damayanti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damayanti "Damayanti"), from the [Mahabharata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabharata "Mahabharata"). Ravi Varma's representation of [Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu "Hindu") characters has become a part of the Indian imagination of the epics. He is often criticized for being too showy and sentimental in his style but his work remains very popular in India. Many of his fabulous paintings are housed at [Laxmi Vilas Palace, Vadodara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laxmi_Vilas_Palace,_Vadodara "Laxmi Vilas Palace, Vadodara").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-11)

**[Thiruvananthapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram "Thiruvananthapuram") Parliamentary (Lok Sabha) Constituency** is one of the 20 parliamentary constituencies in Kerala, India. It is located in [Thiruvananthapuram district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_district "Thiruvananthapuram district") and encompasses the major part of [Thiruvananthapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram "Thiruvananthapuram") city, the capital of [Kerala State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala").

The incumbent MP of this constituency, [Shashi Tharoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor "Shashi Tharoor") of the [Indian National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_National_Congress "Indian National Congress"), has been elected on 4 consecutive occasions: 2009, 2014, 2019 and 2024. He is the longest serving Member of Parliament to have represented the constituency.
This constituency is dominated By [Nair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nair "Nair") and [Nadar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadar_(caste) "Nadar (caste)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_Lok_Sabha_constituency#cite_note-2) As per the electoral roll for the 2024 polls, the total electorate is of 14,03,281 people including 7,27,469 women, 6,75,771 men and 41 transgender people.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_Lok_Sabha_constituency#cite_note-3) Out of total electorate, 26% is rural and 74% is urban.

The Scheduled castes (SC) and Scheduled tribes (ST) is 9.82% and 0.45%, respectively of total electorate.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_Lok_Sabha_constituency#cite_note-4) The constituency also has highest proportion of [Nadars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadar_(caste) "Nadar (caste)") and [Converted Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversion_to_Christianity "Conversion to Christianity") in Kerala.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_Lok_Sabha_constituency#cite_note-5)[Nairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nair "Nair") dominates the urban segments of [Kazhakootam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazhakootam_Assembly_constituency "Kazhakootam Assembly constituency"),[Nemom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nemom_Assembly_constituency "Nemom Assembly constituency"),[Vattiyoorkavu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vattiyoorkavu_Assembly_constituency "Vattiyoorkavu Assembly constituency") and [Thiruvananthapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_Assembly_constituency "Thiruvananthapuram Assembly constituency") While the [Nadars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadar_(caste) "Nadar (caste)") are Concentrated on [Neyyattinkara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neyyattinkara_Assembly_constituency "Neyyattinkara Assembly constituency"),[Parassala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parassala_Assembly_constituency "Parassala Assembly constituency"),[Kovalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kovalam_Assembly_constituency "Kovalam Assembly constituency").

As per the voter list published by the Election commission for the 2019 Lok Sabha elections, there were 13,34,665 voters in the electorate and 1077 polling stations in this constituency.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_Lok_Sabha_constituency#cite_note-ceo.kerala.gov.in-6) The voter turnout for the 2019 Lok Sabha election was 73.45% where as it was 68.63% and 65.74% in the 2014 and 2009 elections respectively.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_Lok_Sabha_constituency#cite_note-7)

Thiruvananthapuram (Malayalam pronunciation: [t̪iɾuʋənən̪d̪ɐˈbuɾəm] ⓘ tirr-ROO-və-nun-Tə-poor-əm), also known as Trivandrum, is the capital city of the Indian state of Kerala.[9][10] As of 2011, the Thiruvananthapuram Municipal Corporation had a population of 957,730 over an area of 214.86 km2,[11] making it the most populous city in Kerala.[12] The larger Thiruvananthapuram metropolitan area has over 1.7 million inhabitants within an area of 543 km2, making it the second-most populous metropolitan area in Kerala after Kochi.[13]. Thiruvananthapuram is one of the few cities in India that serves as a state capital and is also centre for heritage, maritime activities, information technology, research and development, space research, defence, automotive technology, and biosciences. It is also among the few cities in the world where both an international airport and an international seaport are located within the city in close proximity to the city centre.[14]

Located on the west coast of India near the extreme south of the mainland, Thiruvananthapuram is a port city located 10 nautical miles (19 km; 12 mi)[15] from a heavily trafficked east–west shipping channel. The city is home to India's first deep-water trans-shipment port, owned by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram under the Government of Kerala.[16] The city is characterised by its undulating terrain of low coastal hills.[17] Thiruvananthapuram is also known for its cultural heritage, being associated with the musical contributions of Swathi Thirunal Rama Varma and the artistic legacy of painter Raja Ravi Varma. Thiruvananthapuram has contributed to the development of Malayalam literature through individuals like Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer, Kumaran Asan, C. V. Raman Pillai and Narayana Guru. The city is also known for Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, known as the richest temple in the world.[18] The other temples includes the Sreevaraham temple, the Shreekanteswaram temple and the Attukal Bhagavathy temple.
The present regions that constitute Thiruvananthapuram were ruled by the Ays who were related to feudatories of the Chera dynasty.[19] In the 12th century, it was conquered by the Kingdom of Venad.[19] In the 18th century, the king Marthanda Varma expanded the territory, founded the princely state of Travancore and made Thiruvananthapuram its capital.[20] Travancore became the most dominant state in Kerala by defeating the powerful Zamorin of Calicut in the battle of Purakkad in 1755.[21] Following India's independence in 1947, Thiruvananthapuram became the capital of Travancore–Cochin state and remained so until the new Indian state of Kerala was formed in 1956.[22][23]

Thiruvananthapuram is a notable academic and research hub and home to the University of Kerala, APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University, the regional headquarters of Indira Gandhi National Open University, and many other schools and colleges. Thiruvananthapuram is also home to research centres such as the National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology, the Indian Space Research Organisation's Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, the National Centre for Earth Science Studies and a campus of the Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research.[24] Thiruvananthapuram is where India's space programme began, with the headquarters of Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre located there. The city is home to media institutions like Toonz Animation India and Tata Elxsi Ltd, and also to Chitranjali Film Studio, one of the first film studios in Malayalam Cinema, and Kinfra Film and Video Park at Kazhakoottam, which is India's first infotainment industrial park.[25]
In 2012, Thiruvananthapuram was named the best Kerala city to live in, by a field survey conducted by The Times of India.[26] In 2013, the city was ranked the fifteenth best city to live in in India, in a survey conducted by India Today.[27] Thiruvananthapuram was ranked the best Indian city for two consecutive years, 2015 and 2016, according to the Annual Survey of India's City-Systems (ASICS) conducted by the Janaagraha Centre for Citizenship and Democracy.[28] The city was also selected as the best governed city in India in a survey conducted by Janaagraha Centre for citizenship and democracy in 2017.[29]
Etymologyedit

The city takes its name from the Malayalam word thiru-anantha-puram (തിരുവനന്തപുരം [t̪iɾuʋɐnɐn̪d̪ɐpuɾɐm] ⓘ), meaning "The City of Lord Anantha (means infinite, endless, or eternal)",[30] referring to the deity of the Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple located in the city. Thiruvananthapuram is also known in literature, and popular reference as Ananthapuri, derived from the Sanskrit word Syanandurapuram, meaning "The City of Bliss" in Carnatic kirtanas composed by Swathi Thirunal, erstwhile Maharaja of Travancore.[31] The city was officially referred to as Trivandrum until 1991 (Trivandrum being the anglicised name of the town), when the government decided to reinstate the city's original name Thiruvananthapuram. Many Malayalees still refer to the city as Trivandrum, however.[32] The city was also called as Anandapatnam or Anandapatam in Tamil and Telugu, meaning "The City of Ananda" which has the same meaning as the original name. Pre-historic periodedit

Thiruvananthapuram is a relatively modern region with trading traditions dating back to 1000 BCE.[33][34] It is believed that the ships of King Solomon landed in a port then called Ophir (now Poovar) in Thiruvananthapuram in 1036 BCE.[35][36] The city was the trading post for spices, sandalwood and ivory.[37] However, the ancient political and cultural history of the city was almost entirely independent from that of the rest of Kerala. [citation needed]
Ancient periodedit
The southern region of present-day Kerala state (The coastal belt between Thiruvananthapuram and Alappuzha) was under the Ay dynasty, which was more related to the Pandya dynasty of Madurai.[38][page needed] The early rulers of the city were the Ays. Vizhinjam, which is now a region in present-day Thiruvananthapuram, was the capital of the Ay dynasty.[39] Vizhinjam was an important port city from as early as the second century BC.[40][41] During the Ay dynasty's rule, Thiruvananthapuram witnessed many battles in which the Chola and Pandyan dynasties attempted to capture the port town.[42][43]
Middle Agesedit
After the death of king Vikramaditya Varaguna in 925 AD, the glory of the Ays departed and almost all their territories became part of the Chera dynasty.[44][19] During the tenth century, the Cholas attacked and sacked Vizhinjam and surrounding regions.[19] The port in Vizhinjam and the historic education centre of Kanthalloor Sala were also destroyed by Cholas during this period.[45][46] A branch of the Ay family, which had controlled the Padmanabhaswamy Temple, merged with the Kingdom of Venad in the 12th century.[19]

texts.2: Thiruvananthapuram (Malayalam pronunciation: [t̪iɾuʋənən̪d̪ɐˈbuɾəm] ⓘ tirr-ROO-və-nun-Tə-poor-əm), also known as Trivandrum, is the capital city of the Indian state of Kerala.[9][10] As of 2011, the Thiruvananthapuram Municipal Corporation had a population of 957,730 over an area of 214.86 km2,[11] making it the most populous city in Kerala.[12] The larger Thiruvananthapuram metropolitan area has over 1.7 million inhabitants within an area of 543 km2, making it the second-most populous metropolitan area in Kerala after Kochi.[13]. Thiruvananthapuram is one of the few cities in India that serves as a state capital and is also centre for heritage, maritime activities, information technology, research and development, space research, defence, automotive technology, and biosciences. It is also among the few cities in the world where both an international airport and an international seaport are located within the city in close proximity to the city centre.[14]
texts.3:
Located on the west coast of India near the extreme south of the mainland, Thiruvananthapuram is a port city located 10 nautical miles (19 km; 12 mi)[15] from a heavily trafficked east–west shipping channel. The city is home to India's first deep-water trans-shipment port, owned by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram under the Government of Kerala.[16] The city is characterised by its undulating terrain of low coastal hills.[17] Thiruvananthapuram is also known for its cultural heritage, being associated with the musical contributions of Swathi Thirunal Rama Varma and the artistic legacy of painter Raja Ravi Varma. Thiruvananthapuram has contributed to the development of Malayalam literature through individuals like Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer, Kumaran Asan, C. V. Raman Pillai and Narayana Guru. The city is also known for Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, known as the richest temple in the world.[18] The other temples includes the Sreevaraham temple, the Shreekanteswaram temple and the Attukal Bhagavathy temple.
The present regions that constitute Thiruvananthapuram were ruled by the Ays who were related to feudatories of the Chera dynasty.[19] In the 12th century, it was conquered by the Kingdom of Venad.[19] In the 18th century, the king Marthanda Varma expanded the territory, founded the princely state of Travancore and made Thiruvananthapuram its capital.[20] Travancore became the most dominant state in Kerala by defeating the powerful Zamorin of Calicut in the battle of Purakkad in 1755.[21] Following India's independence in 1947, Thiruvananthapuram became the capital of Travancore–Cochin state and remained so until the new Indian state of Kerala was formed in 1956.[22][23]
texts.4:
Thiruvananthapuram is a notable academic and research hub and home to the University of Kerala, APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University, the regional headquarters of Indira Gandhi National Open University, and many other schools and colleges. Thiruvananthapuram is also home to research centres such as the National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology, the Indian Space Research Organisation's Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, the National Centre for Earth Science Studies and a campus of the Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research.[24] Thiruvananthapuram is where India's space programme began, with the headquarters of Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre located there. The city is home to media institutions like Toonz Animation India and Tata Elxsi Ltd, and also to Chitranjali Film Studio, one of the first film studios in Malayalam Cinema, and Kinfra Film and Video Park at Kazhakoottam, which is India's first infotainment industrial park.[25]
In 2012, Thiruvananthapuram was named the best Kerala city to live in, by a field survey conducted by The Times of India.[26] In 2013, the city was ranked the fifteenth best city to live in in India, in a survey conducted by India Today.[27] Thiruvananthapuram was ranked the best Indian city for two consecutive years, 2015 and 2016, according to the Annual Survey of India's City-Systems (ASICS) conducted by the Janaagraha Centre for Citizenship and Democracy.[28] The city was also selected as the best governed city in India in a survey conducted by Janaagraha Centre for citizenship and democracy in 2017.[29]
Etymologyedit
texts.5:
The city takes its name from the Malayalam word thiru-anantha-puram (തിരുവനന്തപുരം [t̪iɾuʋɐnɐn̪d̪ɐpuɾɐm] ⓘ), meaning "The City of Lord Anantha (means infinite, endless, or eternal)",[30] referring to the deity of the Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple located in the city. Thiruvananthapuram is also known in literature, and popular reference as Ananthapuri, derived from the Sanskrit word Syanandurapuram, meaning "The City of Bliss" in Carnatic kirtanas composed by Swathi Thirunal, erstwhile Maharaja of Travancore.[31] The city was officially referred to as Trivandrum until 1991 (Trivandrum being the anglicised name of the town), when the government decided to reinstate the city's original name Thiruvananthapuram. Many Malayalees still refer to the city as Trivandrum, however.[32] The city was also called as Anandapatnam or Anandapatam in Tamil and Telugu, meaning "The City of Ananda" which has the same meaning as the original name. Pre-historic periodedit
texts.6:
Thiruvananthapuram is a relatively modern region with trading traditions dating back to 1000 BCE.[33][34] It is believed that the ships of King Solomon landed in a port then called Ophir (now Poovar) in Thiruvananthapuram in 1036 BCE.[35][36] The city was the trading post for spices, sandalwood and ivory.[37] However, the ancient political and cultural history of the city was almost entirely independent from that of the rest of Kerala. [citation needed]
Ancient periodedit
The southern region of present-day Kerala state (The coastal belt between Thiruvananthapuram and Alappuzha) was under the Ay dynasty, which was more related to the Pandya dynasty of Madurai.[38][page needed] The early rulers of the city were the Ays. Vizhinjam, which is now a region in present-day Thiruvananthapuram, was the capital of the Ay dynasty.[39] Vizhinjam was an important port city from as early as the second century BC.[40][41] During the Ay dynasty's rule, Thiruvananthapuram witnessed many battles in which the Chola and Pandyan dynasties attempted to capture the port town.[42][43]
Middle Agesedit
After the death of king Vikramaditya Varaguna in 925 AD, the glory of the Ays departed and almost all their territories became part of the Chera dynasty.[44][19] During the tenth century, the Cholas attacked and sacked Vizhinjam and surrounding regions.[19] The port in Vizhinjam and the historic education centre of Kanthalloor Sala were also destroyed by Cholas during this period.[45][46] A branch of the Ay family, which had controlled the Padmanabhaswamy Temple, merged with the Kingdom of Venad in the 12th century.[19]

**[Thiruvananthapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram "Thiruvananthapuram") Parliamentary (Lok Sabha) Constituency** is one of the 20 parliamentary constituencies in Kerala, India. It is located in [Thiruvananthapuram district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_district "Thiruvananthapuram district") and encompasses the major part of [Thiruvananthapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram "Thiruvananthapuram") city, the capital of [Kerala State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala").
texts.3:
The incumbent MP of this constituency, [Shashi Tharoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor "Shashi Tharoor") of the [Indian National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_National_Congress "Indian National Congress"), has been elected on 4 consecutive occasions: 2009, 2014, 2019 and 2024. He is the longest serving Member of Parliament to have represented the constituency.
This constituency is dominated By [Nair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nair "Nair") and [Nadar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadar_(caste) "Nadar (caste)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_Lok_Sabha_constituency#cite_note-2) As per the electoral roll for the 2024 polls, the total electorate is of 14,03,281 people including 7,27,469 women, 6,75,771 men and 41 transgender people.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_Lok_Sabha_constituency#cite_note-3) Out of total electorate, 26% is rural and 74% is urban.
texts.4: The Scheduled castes (SC) and Scheduled tribes (ST) is 9.82% and 0.45%, respectively of total electorate.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_Lok_Sabha_constituency#cite_note-4) The constituency also has highest proportion of [Nadars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadar_(caste) "Nadar (caste)") and [Converted Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversion_to_Christianity "Conversion to Christianity") in Kerala.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_Lok_Sabha_constituency#cite_note-5)[Nairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nair "Nair") dominates the urban segments of [Kazhakootam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazhakootam_Assembly_constituency "Kazhakootam Assembly constituency"),[Nemom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nemom_Assembly_constituency "Nemom Assembly constituency"),[Vattiyoorkavu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vattiyoorkavu_Assembly_constituency "Vattiyoorkavu Assembly constituency") and [Thiruvananthapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_Assembly_constituency "Thiruvananthapuram Assembly constituency") While the [Nadars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadar_(caste) "Nadar (caste)") are Concentrated on [Neyyattinkara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neyyattinkara_Assembly_constituency "Neyyattinkara Assembly constituency"),[Parassala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parassala_Assembly_constituency "Parassala Assembly constituency"),[Kovalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kovalam_Assembly_constituency "Kovalam Assembly constituency").

Thiruvananthapuram (Malayalam pronunciation: [t̪iɾuʋənən̪d̪ɐˈbuɾəm] ⓘ tirr-ROO-və-nun-Tə-poor-əm), also known as Trivandrum, is the capital city of the Indian state of Kerala.[9][10] As of 2011, the Thiruvananthapuram Municipal Corporation had a population of 957,730 over an area of 214.86 km2,[11] making it the most populous city in Kerala.[12] The larger Thiruvananthapuram metropolitan area has over 1.7 million inhabitants within an area of 543 km2, making it the second-most populous metropolitan area in Kerala after Kochi.[13]. Thiruvananthapuram is one of the few cities in India that serves as a state capital and is also centre for heritage, maritime activities, information technology, research and development, space research, defence, automotive technology, and biosciences. It is also among the few cities in the world where both an international airport and an international seaport are located within the city in close proximity to the city centre.[14]

Located on the west coast of India near the extreme south of the mainland, Thiruvananthapuram is a port city located 10 nautical miles (19 km; 12 mi)[15] from a heavily trafficked east–west shipping channel. The city is home to India's first deep-water trans-shipment port, owned by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram under the Government of Kerala.[16] The city is characterised by its undulating terrain of low coastal hills.[17] Thiruvananthapuram is also known for its cultural heritage, being associated with the musical contributions of Swathi Thirunal Rama Varma and the artistic legacy of painter Raja Ravi Varma. Thiruvananthapuram has contributed to the development of Malayalam literature through individuals like Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer, Kumaran Asan, C. V. Raman Pillai and Narayana Guru. The city is also known for Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, known as the richest temple in the world.[18] The other temples includes the Sreevaraham temple, the Shreekanteswaram temple and the Attukal Bhagavathy temple.
The present regions that constitute Thiruvananthapuram were ruled by the Ays who were related to feudatories of the Chera dynasty.[19] In the 12th century, it was conquered by the Kingdom of Venad.[19] In the 18th century, the king Marthanda Varma expanded the territory, founded the princely state of Travancore and made Thiruvananthapuram its capital.[20] Travancore became the most dominant state in Kerala by defeating the powerful Zamorin of Calicut in the battle of Purakkad in 1755.[21] Following India's independence in 1947, Thiruvananthapuram became the capital of Travancore–Cochin state and remained so until the new Indian state of Kerala was formed in 1956.[22][23]

Thiruvananthapuram is a notable academic and research hub and home to the University of Kerala, APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University, the regional headquarters of Indira Gandhi National Open University, and many other schools and colleges. Thiruvananthapuram is also home to research centres such as the National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology, the Indian Space Research Organisation's Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, the National Centre for Earth Science Studies and a campus of the Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research.[24] Thiruvananthapuram is where India's space programme began, with the headquarters of Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre located there. The city is home to media institutions like Toonz Animation India and Tata Elxsi Ltd, and also to Chitranjali Film Studio, one of the first film studios in Malayalam Cinema, and Kinfra Film and Video Park at Kazhakoottam, which is India's first infotainment industrial park.[25]
In 2012, Thiruvananthapuram was named the best Kerala city to live in, by a field survey conducted by The Times of India.[26] In 2013, the city was ranked the fifteenth best city to live in in India, in a survey conducted by India Today.[27] Thiruvananthapuram was ranked the best Indian city for two consecutive years, 2015 and 2016, according to the Annual Survey of India's City-Systems (ASICS) conducted by the Janaagraha Centre for Citizenship and Democracy.[28] The city was also selected as the best governed city in India in a survey conducted by Janaagraha Centre for citizenship and democracy in 2017.[29]
Etymologyedit

The city takes its name from the Malayalam word thiru-anantha-puram (തിരുവനന്തപുരം [t̪iɾuʋɐnɐn̪d̪ɐpuɾɐm] ⓘ), meaning "The City of Lord Anantha (means infinite, endless, or eternal)",[30] referring to the deity of the Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple located in the city. Thiruvananthapuram is also known in literature, and popular reference as Ananthapuri, derived from the Sanskrit word Syanandurapuram, meaning "The City of Bliss" in Carnatic kirtanas composed by Swathi Thirunal, erstwhile Maharaja of Travancore.[31] The city was officially referred to as Trivandrum until 1991 (Trivandrum being the anglicised name of the town), when the government decided to reinstate the city's original name Thiruvananthapuram. Many Malayalees still refer to the city as Trivandrum, however.[32] The city was also called as Anandapatnam or Anandapatam in Tamil and Telugu, meaning "The City of Ananda" which has the same meaning as the original name. [citation needed]
